title: Neuroimaging II: MRI & Beyond
summary: MRI sequences, angiography and functional imaging.

lessons.title: MRI Physics Basics

levels.kid:
An MRI machine is a giant magnet shaped like a tunnel. It doesn't use X-rays at all!

Your body is full of water, and water has tiny bits inside called protons that act like little spinning tops. The big magnet makes them all line up. Then the machine sends a radio signal that knocks them over. When they stand back up, they send back a tiny signal, like an echo.

Different body parts send different echoes, and a computer turns them into super detailed pictures. The machine is very loud, and you can't bring anything metal inside because the magnet is so strong!
levels.hs:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) makes pictures using a strong magnet, radio waves and the hydrogen atoms in your body's water and fat. No ionizing radiation is involved.

Here's the idea. Each hydrogen nucleus (a single proton) behaves like a tiny magnet. Inside the scanner's strong field, usually 1.5 or 3 tesla (tens of thousands of times Earth's magnetic field), slightly more protons line up with the field than against it, creating a net magnetization. A radiofrequency (RF) pulse tips that magnetization over. When the pulse stops, the protons relax back and give off a signal the scanner's coils pick up.

Two relaxation processes matter:
- T1 relaxation: how fast magnetization regrows along the main field.
- T2 relaxation: how fast the signal fades as protons fall out of step with each other.

Different tissues relax at different speeds, so by changing timing settings the scanner can make fat, water, gray matter and white matter look brighter or darker. That gives MRI amazing soft-tissue contrast, much better than CT for the brain and spinal cord.

Safety is all about the magnet: metal objects can fly into the scanner, and some implants aren't safe. Scans are loud and take longer than CT, and the tunnel can feel tight.
levels.college:
Hydrogen nuclei have spin and a magnetic moment. In a static field B0, they precess at the Larmor frequency, ω = γB0, where γ for hydrogen is about 42.58 MHz per tesla (so about 64 MHz at 1.5 T and 128 MHz at 3 T). A tiny excess aligned with B0 yields net longitudinal magnetization.

An RF pulse at the Larmor frequency tips magnetization into the transverse plane (a 90-degree pulse in spin echo). Precessing transverse magnetization induces current in receiver coils: the MR signal. Then:
- T1 (longitudinal, spin-lattice) relaxation: recovery of longitudinal magnetization as protons give energy to their surroundings. Fat has short T1; water has long T1.
- T2 (transverse, spin-spin) relaxation: loss of phase coherence from proton-proton interactions. Water has long T2.
- T2*: faster decay including static field inhomogeneities; sensitive to blood products, calcium and air interfaces.

Timing parameters: repetition time (TR) between excitations and echo time (TE) between excitation and signal readout.
- Short TR, short TE: T1-weighted (fat bright, CSF dark).
- Long TR, long TE: T2-weighted (CSF bright).
- Long TR, short TE: proton density weighted.

Spatial encoding uses gradient coils: slice selection, phase encoding and frequency encoding. Data fill k-space, and an inverse Fourier transform produces the image. The center of k-space holds contrast; the periphery holds detail.

Safety: projectile risk from ferromagnetic objects; implants labeled MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe (many modern pacemakers are MR conditional under specific conditions); RF heating measured as specific absorption rate (SAR), higher at 3 T; acoustic noise from gradient switching; and the screened zone system (zones I–IV) controlling access.
levels.phd:
MR signal arises from the bulk magnetization of an enormous number of spins, describable classically by the Bloch equations. At thermal equilibrium the population difference between parallel and antiparallel states follows a Boltzmann distribution and is only a few parts per million at clinical fields, which is why MRI is intrinsically signal-starved and why higher field strengths improve signal-to-noise roughly linearly.

T1 relaxation requires molecular motion with frequency components near the Larmor frequency to allow energy exchange with the lattice. Free water tumbles too fast and bulk solids too slowly, so both relax inefficiently; fat and protein-bound water have motions closer to the Larmor frequency and relax quickly (short T1, bright on T1-weighted images). Paramagnetic agents with unpaired electrons, such as gadolinium or methemoglobin, dramatically accelerate T1 relaxation through dipole-dipole interactions. T1 lengthens with field strength, while T2 is relatively field-independent. T2 decay reflects irreversible dephasing from fluctuating local fields; T2* adds reversible dephasing from static inhomogeneity, which a 180-degree refocusing pulse in spin echo recovers but a gradient echo does not.

Image formation is Fourier encoding. Gradients make precession frequency and phase depend on position, so each sample measures one spatial-frequency component of the object (a point in k-space). Acceleration techniques exploit redundancy: parallel imaging uses the spatial sensitivity of multiple receiver coils to skip k-space lines, and compressed sensing uses sparsity to reconstruct from undersampled data. Each has characteristic artifacts.

Other key artifacts carry physics lessons: chemical shift (fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies, misregistering fat along the frequency direction), susceptibility (local field distortion near metal, air and blood products), aliasing or wrap-around (field of view smaller than the object), and motion ghosts along the phase-encoding direction.
levels.expert:
For a neurosurgeon, MRI is the workhorse for almost everything except acute trauma and acute hemorrhage triage, and safety failures in the MRI suite are among the most preventable catastrophes in a hospital.

Safety discipline:
- Screen every patient, every time, including unconscious patients through family, records and plain films looking for retained metal or fragments near the eyes.
- Know implant status: programmable shunt valves can be reset by the field and need checking and reprogramming afterward; deep brain stimulators, vagus nerve stimulators and spinal cord stimulators are often MR conditional only with specific settings, coils and SAR limits; aneurysm clips must be confirmed MR compatible.
- Ferromagnetic oxygen tanks, monitors and tools must stay out of zone IV. The magnet is always on.
- Patients on ventilators or in intensive care need MR-conditional equipment and a team that has rehearsed emergencies; resuscitation happens outside the scanner room.

Practical choices:
- 3 T gives better signal and resolution, helpful for epilepsy and small pituitary lesions, but worsens susceptibility and heating; 1.5 T can be better around metal.
- Metal artifact reduction sequences help after spinal instrumentation.
- Sedation or anesthesia may be needed for children or claustrophobic patients; plan it ahead.

Reading with physics in mind: know the TR and TE regime of every sequence so you can predict what bright means. Ask whether a hyperintensity is fat, protein, methemoglobin, gadolinium, melanin, calcium in certain states or flow artifact. Recognize pulsation artifacts propagating along the phase direction from the transverse sinuses, which can mimic posterior fossa lesions. When an image doesn't fit the clinical story, artifacts and protocol choices are the first suspects, not exotic diseases.

keyPoints: MRI uses a strong magnet, radiofrequency pulses and hydrogen protons; no ionizing radiation.
Larmor frequency is proportional to field strength (about 42.58 MHz per tesla for hydrogen).
T1 = longitudinal recovery; T2 = transverse decay; T2* also includes field inhomogeneity.
Short TR/TE = T1-weighted; long TR/TE = T2-weighted.
Gradients encode position; data fill k-space and a Fourier transform makes the image.
Safety: projectiles, implants (MR safe/conditional/unsafe), heating (SAR), noise.

lessons.title: Key Sequences

levels.kid:
An MRI can take different kinds of pictures of the same brain, like using different camera filters. Each one is good at finding different problems.

One picture makes brain water dark. Another makes water bright, so swelling shows up. A special one called diffusion shows a fresh stroke as a bright spot within minutes. Another one, called SWI, is great at finding tiny old bleeds, which show up as little black dots.

Doctors put all the pictures together, like clues in a mystery, to figure out what's going on.
levels.hs:
A brain MRI is a set of 'sequences,' each tuned to show different things:

- T1-weighted: good anatomy. CSF is dark, fat is bright. Used with gadolinium contrast to see things that enhance, like tumors.
- T2-weighted: CSF is bright, and so are most problems that contain extra water, such as swelling, inflammation and many tumors.
- FLAIR: a T2 picture with the CSF signal turned off (dark), so bright lesions next to ventricles or in the cortex stand out. Great for multiple sclerosis plaques and edema.
- DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging) with its ADC map: measures how freely water molecules move. In an acute stroke, swollen cells trap water, so the stroke looks bright on DWI and dark on ADC. This shows strokes within minutes, way earlier than CT.
- SWI or GRE: extremely sensitive to iron in blood products and to calcium. Small old bleeds (microbleeds) appear as black dots that 'bloom' bigger than their real size.

Reading a scan means comparing sequences. For example, a spot bright on DWI and dark on ADC is restricted diffusion, most often an acute stroke, but also abscesses and some tumors.
levels.college:
T1-weighted: anatomy and enhancement. Intrinsically T1-bright: fat, methemoglobin (subacute blood), protein-rich fluid, melanin, some calcification, gadolinium, and manganese deposition.

T2-weighted: water-sensitive; most pathology is bright. T2-dark: hemosiderin, deoxyhemoglobin, calcification, flow voids (fast-flowing arteries appear black, a useful sign of patency).

FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery): an inversion pulse timed to null CSF. Periventricular and juxtacortical lesions stand out. Sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity suggests subarachnoid blood, meningitis or leptomeningeal disease (also seen with high inspired oxygen or after gadolinium in renal failure).

DWI/ADC: diffusion gradients dephase moving water; restricted diffusion keeps signal. True restriction: DWI bright and ADC dark. T2 shine-through: DWI bright but ADC also bright (signal carried over from long T2). Restriction occurs in acute infarction (minutes to about 1–2 weeks, with ADC pseudonormalizing in the second week), abscess pus, epidermoid cysts, highly cellular tumors such as lymphoma and medulloblastoma, prion disease (cortical ribboning, basal ganglia), and acute toxic or demyelinating lesions.

SWI/GRE: T2*-sensitive. Microbleeds (hypertensive in deep regions, amyloid angiopathy in lobar regions), cavernous malformations (popcorn lesion with hemosiderin rim), diffuse axonal injury, superficial siderosis, calcification and venous thrombosis. SWI phase images can distinguish calcium (diamagnetic) from blood products (paramagnetic).

Evolution of hematoma signal (T1/T2): hyperacute oxyhemoglobin iso/bright; acute deoxyhemoglobin iso/dark; early subacute intracellular methemoglobin bright/dark; late subacute extracellular methemoglobin bright/bright; chronic hemosiderin rim dark/dark.

DWI-FLAIR mismatch (DWI-positive, FLAIR-negative) suggests an infarct is younger than about 4.5 hours, the basis of imaging-selected thrombolysis in wake-up strokes (WAKE-UP trial).
levels.phd:
Diffusion MRI applies a pair of strong balanced gradients. Stationary spins are dephased then perfectly rephased; spins that move between gradients accumulate residual phase and lose signal. Signal attenuation follows S = S0·exp(−b·ADC), where the b-value encodes gradient strength, duration and separation. ADC is 'apparent' because water in tissue is not free: membranes, organelles and macromolecules hinder and restrict displacement. Early after ischemia, energy failure shifts water from the extracellular to the more restricted intracellular compartment and increases tortuosity of the extracellular space as cells swell, and both mechanisms lower ADC. Because diffusion weighting is built on a T2-weighted echo planar acquisition, long-T2 tissue stays bright even with normal diffusion, the shine-through phenomenon; ADC maps or exponential images remove this confound.

The magnetic behavior of hemoglobin explains blood signal evolution. Oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic. Deoxyhemoglobin has unpaired electrons that cannot approach water closely, so it does not shorten T1, but when confined in intact red cells it creates microscopic field gradients that accelerate T2* and T2 decay. Methemoglobin's ferric iron is accessible to water, enabling dipole-dipole T1 shortening (bright T1); intracellular compartmentalization keeps T2 short until lysis distributes it uniformly, after which T2 lengthens. Hemosiderin and ferritin in macrophages are strongly paramagnetic and compartmentalized, producing persistent T2 and T2* darkening.

Susceptibility-weighted imaging combines magnitude and filtered phase images from a high-resolution 3D gradient echo. Because phase reflects local field shifts, it separates paramagnetic from diamagnetic substances, although the sign depends on vendor convention and geometry. Quantitative susceptibility mapping solves the ill-posed inverse problem from phase to tissue susceptibility, allowing measurement of iron in deep nuclei in neurodegeneration and of oxygen extraction in veins. Blooming exaggerates lesion size, which raises sensitivity while making size estimates unreliable.
levels.expert:
On the reading station, sequences are a conversation. A senior reader asks each one a specific question.

Stroke protocol: DWI/ADC first (is there an infarct, and where?), FLAIR (how old? any DWI-FLAIR mismatch in an unknown-onset stroke?), SWI (hemorrhage, microbleed burden, susceptibility vessel sign marking clot), and MRA or vessel imaging. A stroke MRI can be done in under 10 minutes with abbreviated protocols.

Patterns worth reflexes:
- Restricted diffusion in a ring-enhancing lesion's center: abscess until proven otherwise. Restriction in the enhancing wall but not the necrotic center: tumor more likely.
- Cortical ribboning on DWI with rapidly progressive dementia: think prion disease, but exclude seizures and hypoglycemia, which also restrict.
- Restricted diffusion in an extra-axial lesion that insinuates around vessels: epidermoid. An arachnoid cyst follows CSF on every sequence and doesn't restrict.
- Bilateral posterior FLAIR hyperintensity in a hypertensive or immunosuppressed patient: posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.
- A popcorn lesion with a dark rim on SWI and nearby developmental venous anomaly: cavernous malformation.
- Many lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis in an older adult: amyloid angiopathy, which raises hemorrhage risk and influences antithrombotic decisions.

Pitfalls:
- Assuming DWI-negative means no stroke: small brainstem infarcts can be DWI-negative in the first day, so repeat if the story fits.
- Calling T2 shine-through restriction: always check ADC.
- Misreading sulcal FLAIR signal in an intubated patient on high oxygen as subarachnoid blood.

For operative planning, high-resolution 3D T1 and T2 sequences feed neuronavigation, and the protocol should be ordered with that use in mind.

keyPoints: T1: anatomy and enhancement; fat, methemoglobin, gadolinium bright.
T2: water bright; pathology usually bright; flow voids mark patent arteries.
FLAIR: T2 with CSF nulled; periventricular and cortical lesions stand out.
DWI bright + ADC dark = restricted diffusion (acute infarct, abscess, epidermoid, lymphoma).
SWI/GRE detect blood products and calcium; microbleeds bloom.
DWI-FLAIR mismatch suggests a stroke under about 4.5 hours old.

lessons.title: Contrast Enhancement Patterns

levels.kid:
Your brain has a special wall around its blood vessels, like a security fence. It keeps most things in the blood from getting into the brain.

For some MRI scans, doctors give a special dye called gadolinium through a vein. Normally the fence keeps the dye out of the brain. But if something is wrong, like a tumor or an infection, the fence gets holes. The dye leaks in, and that spot lights up bright on the picture.

The shape of the bright spot, like a ring or a solid ball, gives doctors clues about what the problem is.
levels.hs:
Gadolinium is an MRI contrast agent that makes nearby tissue brighter on T1-weighted images. Normally, the blood-brain barrier (tight seals between the cells lining brain capillaries) keeps gadolinium out of brain tissue. When disease breaks that barrier, the contrast leaks in and the area 'enhances.'

Some normal structures enhance because they don't have a blood-brain barrier: the pituitary gland, choroid plexus, pineal gland and the dura (the tough outer covering).

The pattern of enhancement is a powerful clue:
- Ring enhancement: a bright rim around a darker center. Common causes are brain metastases, abscesses and glioblastoma.
- Solid, uniform enhancement: meningiomas (often with a 'dural tail'), lymphoma and pituitary adenomas.
- Incomplete or open ring: often a large inflammatory demyelinating lesion, like in multiple sclerosis.
- Enhancement along the brain surface: meningitis or cancer spreading in the CSF.
- No enhancement: many low-grade gliomas.

Gadolinium is generally safe, but in people with severe kidney failure some older agents were linked to a rare skin and organ hardening disease, so doctors now favor more stable agents and check kidney function in risky patients.
levels.college:
Gadolinium chelates shorten T1 of nearby water; enhancement on post-contrast T1 reflects blood-brain barrier disruption, increased vascularity, or tissue outside the barrier (dura, pituitary, choroid plexus, pineal, area postrema, circumventricular organs).

Ring enhancement differential (mnemonic MAGIC DR): Metastasis, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct (subacute), Contusion, Demyelination, Radiation necrosis. Discriminators:
- Abscess: smooth, thin ring, often thinner on the ventricular side (less oxygenated, less fibroblast collagen), central restricted diffusion.
- Glioblastoma: thick, irregular, nodular ring, central necrosis, infiltrative T2/FLAIR signal, may cross the corpus callosum (butterfly pattern).
- Metastases: often multiple, at the gray-white junction, with edema out of proportion to size.
- Demyelination: incomplete ring, open toward gray matter.
- Radiation necrosis: in the treated field, 'soap bubble' or 'Swiss cheese' enhancement, low perfusion.

Homogeneous enhancement: meningioma (extra-axial, dural tail, CSF cleft), primary CNS lymphoma (periventricular, restricted diffusion, may cross the corpus callosum), schwannoma (vestibular, ice-cream-cone shape at the internal auditory canal), pituitary adenoma.

Meningeal patterns: pachymeningeal (dura-arachnoid; smooth diffuse in intracranial hypotension or post-surgery, nodular in tumors) versus leptomeningeal (pia-arachnoid following sulci; meningitis, carcinomatosis, sarcoidosis).

Gyriform enhancement appears in subacute infarcts (the '2-2-2 rule': starts around 2 days, peaks around 2 weeks, fades by about 2 months).

After glioma chemoradiation, new enhancement within about 3 months may be pseudoprogression rather than true progression; RANO criteria guide interpretation, and perfusion imaging helps.

Safety: nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with older linear agents in severe renal impairment; gadolinium deposition in the dentate nucleus and globus pallidus after repeated linear-agent doses, of unclear clinical significance. Macrocyclic agents are preferred.
levels.phd:
Enhancement is a kinetic phenomenon governed by perfusion, capillary permeability-surface area product and the extravascular extracellular space. Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI models this with compartmental pharmacokinetics; the Tofts model estimates Ktrans (transfer from plasma to the extravascular space), ve (extravascular extracellular volume fraction) and vp. In a leaky tumor, Ktrans reflects permeability and flow combined, and these parameters can track response to antiangiogenic therapy. Static post-contrast T1 imaging collapses all of this into a single time point, which is why timing after injection influences appearance: small metastases conspicuity improves with delayed imaging, and some lesions show slow, progressive fill-in.

Enhancement is not equivalent to tumor. In high-grade gliomas, infiltrating cells extend well beyond the enhancing rim into nonenhancing T2/FLAIR signal, the biological reason why gross total resection of enhancement is not cure and why supramaximal resection of FLAIR abnormality is studied. Conversely, antiangiogenic agents such as bevacizumab rapidly restore barrier tightness and reduce enhancement and edema without necessarily killing tumor cells, the 'pseudoresponse.' Response criteria therefore incorporate nonenhancing disease, clinical status and corticosteroid use.

The relaxivity of a gadolinium agent depends on the number of inner-sphere water molecules, their exchange rate and the rotational correlation time of the complex. Macrocyclic chelates are kinetically inert, releasing far less free gadolinium than linear agents; free gadolinium is toxic and can precipitate in tissues. Deposition findings (T1 hyperintensity of the dentate nucleus after repeated linear-agent exposure) shifted practice, and the regulatory restriction of several linear agents followed.

Distinguishing recurrence from treatment effect remains a research frontier, combining DSC perfusion (rCBV), DCE permeability, diffusion, spectroscopy and amino acid PET, increasingly with radiomics and machine learning, though prospective validation remains limited.
levels.expert:
Contrast is how I find most lesions that matter for surgery, and the pattern often decides the next step before pathology.

A ring-enhancing lesion workflow:
- Look at DWI first. Central restriction with a smooth thin wall points to abscess: urgent neurosurgery and infectious disease, aspiration or excision, and a search for the source (dental, sinus, cardiac, lung).
- Multiple lesions at the gray-white junction: search for a primary cancer with body imaging before biopsying the brain, if the patient is stable.
- A single thick, irregular rim with infiltrative FLAIR signal: likely glioblastoma; plan maximal safe resection with mapping when near eloquent cortex.
- Suspected lymphoma: homogeneous periventricular enhancement with restriction. Avoid starting corticosteroids before biopsy if the patient is stable, because steroids can shrink lymphoma and make the biopsy nondiagnostic.

Practical points:
- Always acquire pre-contrast T1. Intrinsic T1 brightness (blood, fat, melanin, protein) can be mistaken for enhancement.
- Use volumetric 3D post-contrast T1 for navigation and for small metastasis detection before radiosurgery.
- Early postoperative MRI, ideally within about 48 to 72 hours, establishes extent of resection before reactive enhancement develops.
- In treated gliomas, be careful about new enhancement in the first months after chemoradiation; pseudoprogression is common, particularly in tumors with MGMT promoter methylation.
- Diffuse smooth dural enhancement, sagging brain, and engorged venous sinuses with orthostatic headache suggest intracranial hypotension from a CSF leak, not meningitis or tumor.

Gadolinium decisions: macrocyclic agents, the lowest needed exposure in patients needing many scans, careful thought in severe kidney disease and in pregnancy, and an imaging plan that answers the clinical question in as few contrast studies as possible.

keyPoints: Enhancement = blood-brain barrier breakdown, high vascularity, or structures without a barrier (dura, pituitary, choroid plexus, pineal).
Ring enhancement: metastasis, abscess, glioblastoma, subacute infarct, contusion, demyelination, radiation necrosis.
Abscess: thin smooth ring with central restricted diffusion; GBM: thick irregular ring.
Open ring suggests demyelination; dural tail suggests meningioma.
Pseudoprogression can mimic glioma progression within about 3 months of chemoradiation.
Macrocyclic gadolinium agents are preferred for safety.

lessons.title: Angiography

levels.kid:
Angiography means taking pictures of blood vessels. One way is with a tiny, soft tube called a catheter. A doctor slides it into a blood vessel in the leg or wrist and gently guides it all the way up to the neck.

Then they squirt in dye and take fast X-ray movies. The blood vessels light up like a tree with branches, and doctors can watch blood flowing in real time!

Even cooler, the same tube can be used to fix problems, like pulling out a clot or filling a weak bulge in a vessel with tiny coils.
levels.hs:
Angiography is imaging of blood vessels, and there are three main ways to do it in the brain:

- CT angiography (CTA): a fast CT with contrast dye. Quick and great in emergencies.
- MR angiography (MRA): can be done without any dye using a technique called time-of-flight, which makes flowing blood bright. Good for screening, though it can overestimate narrowing.
- Digital subtraction angiography (DSA): the gold standard. A catheter is threaded from an artery in the groin or wrist up to the neck arteries. Dye is injected while X-ray images are taken very fast. The computer subtracts the bones from the image, leaving just the vessels.

DSA shows tiny details and blood flow over time, like watching a movie. It's used to find and measure aneurysms, study arteriovenous malformations (AVMs, abnormal tangles where arteries connect straight into veins), find tears in artery walls, and see narrowing.

DSA can also treat disease. Through the same catheter, doctors can pull out stroke clots (thrombectomy), fill aneurysms with coils, or block abnormal vessels with glue-like materials. The risks are small but real, like bleeding at the puncture site or, rarely, a stroke.
levels.college:
Digital subtraction angiography: arterial access (femoral or increasingly radial), selective catheterization of carotid and vertebral arteries, contrast injection with rapid serial imaging. A mask image before contrast is subtracted to remove bone. Arterial, capillary and venous phases provide temporal information. 3D rotational angiography generates volumetric reconstructions for aneurysm neck and branch analysis.

MRA: time-of-flight (TOF) relies on inflow of unsaturated spins; no contrast needed. Limitations: overestimates stenosis from turbulent flow dephasing, signal loss in slow or in-plane flow, and T1-bright material (subacute thrombus, fat) can mimic flow. Contrast-enhanced MRA is faster and less flow-dependent. Phase-contrast MRA measures velocity and direction.

Indications and findings:
- Aneurysms: size, neck, dome-to-neck ratio, relationship to branches; guides coiling versus clipping.
- AVMs: feeding arteries, nidus, draining veins with early venous filling. Spetzler-Martin grade: size (under 3, 3–6, over 6 centimeters: 1–3 points), eloquence of adjacent brain (0–1), deep venous drainage (0–1); total 1–5 predicts surgical risk.
- Dural arteriovenous fistulas: arterial feeders to a dural sinus or cortical vein; cortical venous reflux signals hemorrhage risk.
- Dissection: tapered narrowing ('string sign'), flame-shaped occlusion, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm.
- Moyamoya: progressive distal ICA stenosis with a 'puff of smoke' of collateral vessels.
- Vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage, carotid stenosis grading (NASCET method), venous sinus thrombosis.

Complications of diagnostic DSA: access site hematoma, retroperitoneal hemorrhage (femoral), arterial dissection, thromboembolic stroke (permanent neurologic deficit uncommon, well under 1 percent in modern series), contrast reaction and contrast-associated kidney injury.
levels.phd:
Time-of-flight MRA exploits saturation physics. Stationary tissue in a slab receives rapid repeated RF pulses with short TR and becomes saturated, contributing little signal. Fresh, unsaturated blood flowing into the slab carries full longitudinal magnetization and appears bright. Signal therefore depends on velocity, direction relative to the slab and the slab thickness; slow flow or flow within the slab plane saturates. Turbulence and acceleration downstream of a stenosis cause intravoxel phase dispersion and signal void, which explains why TOF exaggerates stenosis and can mimic occlusion. Multiple overlapping thin-slab acquisition and tilted optimized nonsaturating excitation mitigate these effects. Phase-contrast techniques encode velocity in the phase of the signal using bipolar gradients, enabling quantitative flow, useful for collateral and shunt assessment and 4D flow research on aneurysm hemodynamics.

DSA's temporal resolution matters biologically. AV shunting is defined dynamically: venous opacification during the arterial phase indicates a direct arteriovenous connection without an intervening capillary bed. Flow-related aneurysms on AVM feeders, intranidal aneurysms and venous outflow stenosis are angioarchitectural features associated with hemorrhage risk. In dural AV fistulas, the Borden and Cognard classifications are built on venous drainage pattern, and cortical venous reflux predicts aggressive behavior.

Hemodynamics underpin aneurysm biology. Computational fluid dynamics derived from 3D angiography estimates wall shear stress and oscillatory shear; both low, oscillatory shear (associated with inflammatory, atherosclerotic walls) and high, impinging flow (associated with mural cell loss) have been linked to growth and rupture in different aneurysm phenotypes. Vessel-wall MRI, showing aneurysm wall enhancement, is a proposed marker of inflammation and instability, though not yet a validated decision tool. The angiogram is thus not just a map but a window onto the physics shaping disease.
levels.expert:
The modern cerebrovascular neurosurgeon often holds both a microscope and a catheter, and angiography is where many decisions get made.

Choosing the test:
- Emergency stroke: CTA, then DSA as part of thrombectomy.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage with a negative CTA: DSA, because small aneurysms, dissections and dural fistulas can hide; repeat DSA in a week or so if still negative and the pattern isn't perimesencephalic.
- Young patient with a lobar hemorrhage and no clear cause: DSA, sometimes after the clot resolves, to find a small AVM compressed by hematoma.
- Screening relatives in familial aneurysm syndromes: MRA without contrast.
- Follow-up of coiled aneurysms: MRA often suffices, with DSA when recurrence is suspected. Clips cause artifacts on CTA and MRA.

Reading DSA like an operator:
- Get at least two orthogonal views and 3D rotational images for every aneurysm: neck width, incorporated branches and the projection of the dome decide coiling, stent assistance, flow diversion or clipping.
- For AVMs, identify every feeder, the nidus compactness and all draining veins, especially deep drainage. Spetzler-Martin grade guides surgery versus radiosurgery versus observation.
- Always look at the venous phase. Delayed venous drainage, venous congestion and sinus thrombosis are easy to miss when focused on arteries.
- In vasospasm, compare with the baseline angiogram; intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty are options for symptomatic spasm.

Procedural safety: meticulous flushing and air elimination, anticoagulation during intervention per protocol, and post-procedure access-site checks. Radial access lowers access-site bleeding. A post-angiogram new deficit is a stroke until proven otherwise: immediate exam, imaging and, if needed, a return to the angiography suite.

keyPoints: DSA (catheter angiography) is the gold standard: high resolution, dynamic, and therapeutic.
TOF MRA needs no contrast but overestimates stenosis and depends on flow.
AVM = arteries connecting directly to veins via a nidus; early venous drainage on DSA.
Spetzler-Martin grade: size, eloquence, deep venous drainage (1–5).
Dissection: string sign, flame tapering, pseudoaneurysm; moyamoya: 'puff of smoke'.
DSA complications: access-site bleeding, dissection, rarely stroke.

lessons.title: Functional & Advanced Imaging

levels.kid:
Some brain scans don't just show what the brain looks like. They show what the brain is doing!

When you wiggle your fingers, the part of your brain that moves them works harder and needs more blood. A special MRI called fMRI can see that extra blood, so that spot lights up.

Another scan draws the brain's wires, the long cables connecting different areas, in pretty colors. Surgeons use these maps like a GPS so they can remove a tumor while staying away from the parts that help you talk and move.
levels.hs:
Advanced imaging shows how the brain works, not just its shape.

- Functional MRI (fMRI): when a brain area becomes active, blood flow to it increases more than its oxygen use. That changes the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin, which slightly changes the MRI signal (the BOLD signal). By having patients tap fingers or name pictures during the scan, doctors can map movement and language areas before surgery.
- Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and tractography: water moves more easily along nerve fibers than across them. Measuring that direction lets computers draw the brain's white matter tracts, like the corticospinal tract for movement.
- MR spectroscopy: measures chemicals in tissue. Tumors often have high choline (from cells dividing) and low NAA (a marker of healthy neurons).
- PET scans: a small amount of radioactive tracer shows activity. FDG PET shows sugar use; areas causing seizures often use less sugar between seizures. Other PET tracers show amyloid or tau proteins in Alzheimer's disease.
- DaT-SPECT shows dopamine nerve endings, helping tell Parkinson's disease from other tremors.

Surgeons combine these maps with neuronavigation, a GPS-like system, to plan safe paths through the brain. But maps can be imperfect, so for surgery near critical areas they may also test the brain directly during an awake operation.
levels.college:
fMRI BOLD: neural activity triggers neurovascular coupling; cerebral blood flow rises more than oxygen consumption, so deoxyhemoglobin (paramagnetic) concentration falls and T2*-weighted signal rises a few percent, peaking about 4–6 seconds after activity (the hemodynamic response function). Task fMRI maps motor cortex and language lateralization; resting-state fMRI maps intrinsic networks (for example the default mode network).

DTI: diffusion measured in at least six directions defines a tensor per voxel. Fractional anisotropy (FA) quantifies directionality (high in compact tracts like the corpus callosum and internal capsule); mean diffusivity quantifies overall diffusion. Tractography follows principal eigenvectors to reconstruct tracts (corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus, optic radiations including Meyer's loop). Limitation: crossing fibers; advanced models (HARDI, constrained spherical deconvolution) help.

MR spectroscopy peaks: NAA (neuronal integrity), choline (membrane turnover, high in tumors), creatine (energy reference), lactate (anaerobic metabolism, doublet), lipids (necrosis), myo-inositol, and 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG), an oncometabolite in IDH-mutant gliomas. High choline/NAA ratio suggests tumor; abscess may show amino acids, acetate and succinate.

Perfusion MRI: DSC (dynamic susceptibility contrast) gives relative CBV, elevated in high-grade tumors and low in radiation necrosis; arterial spin labeling (ASL) measures flow without contrast.

Nuclear medicine: FDG PET (interictal hypometabolism in epileptogenic zones; temporoparietal hypometabolism in Alzheimer disease; frontotemporal in frontotemporal dementia); amyloid and tau PET; amino acid PET for gliomas; ictal SPECT shows hyperperfusion at seizure onset (SISCOM subtracts interictal from ictal and co-registers to MRI); DaT-SPECT shows loss of striatal dopamine transporter in parkinsonian syndromes.

MEG (magnetoencephalography) localizes interictal spikes and maps eloquent cortex with millisecond resolution.
levels.phd:
The BOLD signal is an indirect, vascular proxy for neural activity. Logothetis and colleagues showed it correlates better with local field potentials, reflecting synaptic input and local processing, than with spiking output. Neurovascular coupling is mediated by astrocytes, pericytes and neuronal signaling molecules including nitric oxide, prostaglandins and potassium, and its flow overshoot relative to oxygen consumption is why active regions become relatively oxygenated. Because the response is slow and spatially blurred by draining veins, BOLD localizes to millimeters and seconds; high-field (7 T) and layer-specific fMRI push toward cortical columns and laminae.

The clinical implication is neurovascular uncoupling. Near high-grade gliomas and arteriovenous malformations, abnormal vessels and tumor-induced astrocyte dysfunction blunt the hemodynamic response, so eloquent cortex can be functionally active yet show little BOLD signal: a dangerous false negative for the surgeon. Task fMRI also identifies regions involved in a task, not regions essential for it; resection of a 'lit' area may cause no deficit, while resection of a quiet area can. Direct electrical stimulation remains the causal gold standard.

Diffusion tractography inherits model limitations. The single-tensor model fails in the majority of white matter voxels that contain crossing, kissing or fanning fibers, and deterministic tractography can generate anatomically implausible streamlines while missing true ones; validation challenges have shown high false-positive rates across algorithms. Probabilistic methods and multi-shell acquisitions improve estimation but do not convert streamlines into proven axonal connections.

Molecular imaging connects biology to images: amyloid and tau PET enabled biological definitions of Alzheimer disease and patient selection for anti-amyloid antibodies; 2HG spectroscopy offers noninvasive IDH status; and PET tracers targeting translocator protein image neuroinflammation. The frontier merges these modalities with machine learning, but the scientific discipline remains understanding what each signal physically measures.
levels.expert:
Functional and advanced imaging changed what is resectable, but every map comes with error bars that a surgeon must respect.

Planning an operation near eloquent cortex:
- Task fMRI for language lateralization and rough localization of motor and language areas; correlate with the patient's handedness and deficits.
- DTI tractography of the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus and optic radiations, displayed in neuronavigation to plan an entry corridor.
- Remember brain shift: once the dura opens and CSF drains or tumor is removed, the brain moves by millimeters to centimeters, so preoperative maps drift. Intraoperative MRI or ultrasound can update the picture.
- For tumors in language or motor areas, awake craniotomy with direct cortical and subcortical stimulation, plus motor evoked potentials, provides the real-time causal map. Resect to functional boundaries, not just imaging boundaries.

Epilepsy surgery is multimodal by design: MRI (often at 3 T with an epilepsy protocol), video-EEG, FDG PET, ictal SPECT with SISCOM, MEG and neuropsychological testing build a hypothesis of the epileptogenic zone; when they disagree, stereo-EEG electrodes test it directly. Concordance between modalities predicts seizure freedom after resection.

Tumor follow-up: when new enhancement appears after treatment, combine perfusion (high rCBV favors tumor), diffusion, spectroscopy and, where available, amino acid PET. No single modality is definitive; trends over time and multidisciplinary review matter.

Movement disorders: DaT-SPECT confirms presynaptic dopaminergic loss but doesn't distinguish Parkinson disease from atypical parkinsonism well; structural MRI with specific sequences and clinical evaluation fill the gap. For deep brain stimulation, high-resolution imaging allows direct targeting of nuclei like the subthalamic nucleus.

Explaining limits to patients and families honestly is part of the job: a colored tract on a screen is a model, not a promise.

keyPoints: fMRI BOLD reflects blood oxygenation changes from neurovascular coupling, not neurons directly.
Neurovascular uncoupling near tumors can cause false-negative fMRI.
DTI measures directional diffusion; FA reflects tract integrity; tractography struggles with crossing fibers.
MR spectroscopy: tumors show high choline and low NAA; 2HG marks IDH-mutant gliomas.
FDG PET: interictal hypometabolism at seizure focus; ictal SPECT shows hyperperfusion.
Direct cortical stimulation in awake surgery remains the causal gold standard.
